Chapter 1: WEBSITE LIFECYCLE AND PLANNING

Chapter 1: WEBSITE LIFECYCLE AND PLANNING

This chapter covers the website lifecycle, planning a website release, roles and responsibilities, and preparing a release checklist. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

1.1 The Website Lifecycle

Detailed lesson: A release is not the end of a website project. Requirements can change, users can discover defects, and browsers can introduce new behavior. Teams should plan how the website will be checked after launch and who will make corrections.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

A website lifecycle includes planning, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. These stages are connected: a change made during maintenance may require new testing before it is published.

Practical Application

For a school website, a developer might create a course page, test its links and forms, upload it to hosting, and monitor reports of missing resources. The work does not end when the URL becomes public.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

1.2 Planning a Website Release

Detailed lesson: A release plan should identify the exact version, the expected changes, the deployment method, and the person responsible for approval. A rollback plan explains how to restore a working version if the update fails.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Release planning identifies what will be published, who will approve it, which hosting environment will be used, and what evidence will show that the release is ready. It should also define a recovery plan if the published version fails.

Practical Application

Chapter 1: WEBSITE LIFECYCLE AND PLANNING · Continued

Record the release date, project version, files being changed, domain, responsible person, and expected user-facing behavior. Keep a copy of the previously working website.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

1.3 Roles and Responsibilities

Detailed lesson: Clear responsibilities prevent changes from being lost between content writers, testers, and developers. Even a small team benefits from naming the person who verifies a release and the person who can restore an earlier version.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

A small team may combine roles, but responsibilities should remain clear. Content contributors prepare information, designers plan its presentation, developers implement features, reviewers check quality, and an editor authorizes publication.

Practical Application

A two-person student team can assign one member to build and deploy the site and another to review content and test features. Both should know who can approve changes.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

1.4 Preparing a Release Checklist

Detailed lesson: A useful checklist is specific and repeatable: test navigation, images, forms, mobile layout, accessibility, and downloads. Record the result for each item and investigate any failed check before publishing.

Chapter 1: WEBSITE LIFECYCLE AND PLANNING · Continued

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

A release checklist reduces avoidable mistakes. It should include content accuracy, working navigation, accessible forms, responsive layout, valid links, configuration, backups, and a final live-site review.

Practical Application

Check the homepage, a representative internal page, an image-heavy page, and each important form before and after publication.

Key Considerations

Chapter 2: WEBSITE TESTING FUNDAMENTALS

Chapter 2: WEBSITE TESTING FUNDAMENTALS

This chapter covers purpose of website testing, functional and content testing, usability and accessibility testing, compatibility and responsive testing, and performance and security testing. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

2.1 Purpose of Website Testing

Detailed lesson: Testing compares expected behavior with observed behavior. A good test includes a starting condition, a user action, an expected result, and an actual result. A failed test becomes a defect report.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Website testing checks whether a site behaves as intended and serves its users reliably. It detects defects before publication and provides evidence that important requirements have been met.

Practical Application

Testing a registration page includes valid input, missing required fields, incorrect email formats, successful submission, and appropriate error messages.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

2.2 Functional and Content Testing

Detailed lesson: Functional tests should cover both normal and unusual inputs. A library search should find matching titles, handle an empty query, and show a clear message when there are no matches. Content tests verify accuracy and working links.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Functional testing checks buttons, menus, search, links, forms, downloads, and application logic. Content testing checks spelling, accuracy, headings, images, and whether information is complete and current.

Practical Application

Chapter 2: WEBSITE TESTING FUNDAMENTALS · Continued

A book library website should open the correct book when its cover is selected and show the expected lesson after navigation. Every cover should match the linked book.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

2.3 Usability and Accessibility Testing

Detailed lesson: Test with keyboard navigation, zoomed text, and different viewport sizes. Controls should have understandable names, visible focus, and predictable behavior. Accessibility improves usability for many people, not only users of assistive technology.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Usability testing asks whether people can understand and complete tasks. Accessibility testing checks whether people with different abilities and assistive technologies can use the interface.

Practical Application

Navigate the site using only a keyboard. Check visible focus, form labels, meaningful alternative text, readable contrast, and clear error messages.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

2.4 Compatibility and Responsive Testing

Detailed lesson: Responsive testing checks whether content rearranges without becoming hidden or difficult to use. Compare narrow phones, tablets, and desktop screens, and verify at least the browsers used by the intended audience.

Chapter 2: WEBSITE TESTING FUNDAMENTALS · Continued

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

A website can look correct on one computer but fail on another browser or screen size. Compatibility testing examines rendering and behavior across supported environments; responsive testing examines adaptation to changing viewport widths.

Practical Application

Check desktop and mobile widths. Ensure menus remain reachable, images fit their containers, and tables do not hide important information.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

2.5 Performance and Security Testing

Detailed lesson: Large images, unnecessary scripts, and blocking resources can slow a website. Security checks include HTTPS, safe input handling, dependency updates, and access controls for protected functions. Test only systems you are authorized to assess.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Performance testing observes loading speed, responsiveness, and stability under expected conditions. Security testing examines weaknesses that could expose information or allow unintended actions.

Practical Application

Optimize large images, inspect network requests, test authentication and permissions where applicable, and never publish passwords or private configuration files.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

Chapter 3: WEBSITE QUALITY ASSURANCE

Chapter 3: WEBSITE QUALITY ASSURANCE

This chapter covers quality assurance and testing, recording and prioritizing issues, retesting and regression testing, and release acceptance. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

3.1 Quality Assurance and Testing

Detailed lesson: Quality assurance improves the development process, while testing checks the product. Code reviews, consistent naming, release checklists, and test plans help prevent defects before they reach users.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Quality assurance is the broader process of preventing and detecting quality problems. Testing is one activity within that process. QA also includes standards, review procedures, documentation, and issue follow-up.

Practical Application

The maintenance source lists broken links, missing images, browser titles, metadata, oversized pages, compatibility, application functionality, and accessibility as quality checkpoints.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

Quality checkpoints from the maintenance source include broken links, missing images, missing page titles, spelling errors, missing metadata, oversized pages, browser compatibility, application behavior, legal obligations, accessibility, and design consistency.

3.2 Recording and Prioritizing Issues

Detailed lesson: A defect report should include steps to reproduce, the expected result, the actual result, the environment, and a screenshot when useful. Prioritize issues based on impact and urgency rather than appearance alone.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Chapter 3: WEBSITE QUALITY ASSURANCE · Continued

A useful issue log identifies the affected page, steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result, severity, evidence, and person responsible. Consistent records make defects easier to resolve.

Practical Application

An issue titled “Download button opens wrong PDF” should specify the exact page and link, the expected file, and the incorrect file actually opened.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

3.3 Retesting and Regression Testing

Detailed lesson: Retesting confirms that a specific defect is fixed. Regression testing checks whether the fix damaged another feature. After changing navigation code, test the corrected link and the other links that share the same component.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Retesting confirms that a specific defect was corrected. Regression testing checks whether a change unintentionally damaged features that previously worked. Both are important after code or content updates.

Practical Application

After repairing a navigation menu, test the repaired link and also verify that the other menu links still work.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

3.4 Release Acceptance

Detailed lesson: Acceptance criteria describe what must work before a website is approved for publication. Criteria should be observable, such as all required pages opening, forms showing validation messages, and images loading correctly.

Chapter 3: WEBSITE QUALITY ASSURANCE · Continued

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Release acceptance is a documented decision that a website is sufficiently ready for its intended use. Not every minor imperfection must block release, but serious functional, security, and accessibility problems should be addressed.

Practical Application

A school project may require all major pages to load, no broken essential links, working search, and successful mobile navigation before approval.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. Chapter 4: WEB HOSTING FUNDAMENTALS

Chapter 4: WEB HOSTING FUNDAMENTALS

This chapter covers what web hosting provides, hosting models and resources, choosing a hosting provider, and domain names and dns. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

4.1 What Web Hosting Provides

Detailed lesson: A hosting service stores website files and makes them available over a network. The host serves requests for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other resources. Hosting choices depend on whether a site is static or needs server-side processing.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Web hosting makes website files or applications available through servers connected to the Internet. A hosting environment may provide storage, web server software, networking, certificates, backups, and administration tools.

Practical Application

A static HTML website needs a service that can serve its files. A database-driven website also needs compatible application and database services.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

4.2 Hosting Models and Resources

Detailed lesson: Shared hosting, virtual private servers, managed platforms, and static hosting services offer different levels of control. Compare storage, bandwidth, security responsibilities, deployment options, and expected traffic.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Common hosting approaches include shared hosting, virtual private servers, dedicated servers, managed platforms, and static-site hosting. They differ in control, operational responsibility, scalability, and cost.

Practical Application

Chapter 4: WEB HOSTING FUNDAMENTALS · Continued

Choose a platform based on project needs rather than assuming that the most expensive option is best. A small student site may not require a dedicated server.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. 4.3 Choosing a Hosting Provider

Detailed lesson: Evaluate reliability, documentation, support, backup options, HTTPS support, pricing, and ease of updating files. A student project may favor a simple static deployment workflow, while a database-backed application needs additional services.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

A hosting provider should be evaluated for reliability, support, security, performance, available tools, storage, bandwidth policy, backups, and compatibility with the site. The historical slide source emphasizes selecting a provider based on practical needs and support.

Compare features and current terms before subscribing. Prices and brand recommendations in older presentations may no longer be accurate.

4.4 Domain Names and DNS

Detailed lesson: A domain is a human-readable name used to reach a website. DNS records direct visitors to the correct hosting destination. DNS changes can take time to become visible because resolvers cache earlier answers.

Chapter 4: WEB HOSTING FUNDAMENTALS · Continued

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

A domain name is a human-readable identifier such as example.org. DNS translates domain names into records used to reach hosting services. Domain registration and web hosting are related but separate services.

Practical Application

A domain may point to a hosting platform through A, AAAA, or CNAME records. Changes can take time to become visible because of DNS caching.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. Detailed lesson: Control panels help administrators manage files, domains, certificates, and sometimes databases. Their features vary by provider. Limit access to authorized users and protect accounts with strong authentication.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

A hosting control panel offers tools for managing files, domains, email accounts, databases, certificates, and other services. The exact interface varies by provider and version.

5.2 Organizing Website Files

Detailed lesson: Keep a consistent folder structure for pages, scripts, stylesheets, and images. Relative paths depend on file locations. A broken image after deployment often indicates a filename, capitalization, or path mismatch.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

A consistent folder structure helps prevent missing assets and incorrect paths. Keep HTML pages, stylesheets, scripts, images, and downloads in predictable locations.

Practical Application

Chapter 5: HOSTING CONFIGURATION AND FILE TRANSFER · Continued

For example, place CSS in assets/css, scripts in assets/js, and pictures in assets/images. Confirm that relative paths match the published folder structure.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. 5.3 Uploading Through a File Manager

Detailed lesson: When uploading files manually, preserve directory structure and verify that the server contains the latest versions. Uploading only one HTML page without its CSS or images can make the published site look incomplete.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

A browser-based file manager lets authorized users upload, rename, move, and delete files on a hosting server. It is convenient for small updates but may be less efficient for many files.

Practical Application

Upload the homepage and its supporting assets to the correct public directory. Check that the server serves the intended index file and that no sensitive files are public.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. 5.4 FTP, FTPS and SFTP

Detailed lesson: FTP is an older file transfer protocol that does not protect credentials by default. FTPS adds TLS to FTP, while SFTP uses SSH. Use a secure method supported by the hosting provider.

Chapter 5: HOSTING CONFIGURATION AND FILE TRANSFER · Continued

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

File-transfer tools can move files between a local computer and a server. FTP is an older unencrypted protocol; FTPS adds TLS protection; SFTP operates over SSH. Prefer secure transfer options when supported.

Practical Application

The source demonstrates FileZilla as a graphical client. Modern setup should use the secure protocol and connection details supplied by the hosting provider.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. 5.5 Verifying Files on the Server

Detailed lesson: After uploading, open the live website rather than relying only on the upload success message. Test direct links to internal pages, check images, and review browser developer tools for missing resources.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Successful upload does not guarantee a working website. File names, permissions, directory paths, and references must all be correct. A live-site check verifies that visitors can actually use the deployed content.

Practical Application

Open the public URL in a private browser window. Inspect images, scripts, styles, navigation, and downloads rather than checking only the homepage.

Chapter 6: WEBSITE DEPLOYMENT

Chapter 6: WEBSITE DEPLOYMENT

This chapter covers deployment preparation, step-by-step website publication, version control and automated deployment, and deployment verification and rollback. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

6.1 Deployment Preparation

Detailed lesson: Before publishing, remove test credentials and unused files, confirm configuration values, and create a recoverable copy of the last working version. A release should be reproducible from known source files.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Deployment preparation includes building the final version, checking environment settings, validating assets, protecting credentials, and ensuring that a backup or previous release is available.

Practical Application

Separate local development settings from production settings. Never embed database passwords or API secrets in public frontend files.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

6.2 Step-by-Step Website Publication

Detailed lesson: A basic publication process includes preparing files, connecting the project to hosting, configuring the domain, deploying, and testing the public URL. Document each step so another team member can repeat it.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Traditional deployment may involve connecting to a hosting server, choosing the public directory, transferring files, and opening the live URL. The supplied slides illustrate this workflow with a file-transfer client.

6.3 Version Control and Automated Deployment

Detailed lesson: Version control records changes and supports collaboration. A hosting platform can build and publish a new version after a change is pushed to a connected repository. Review changes before merging into the production branch.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Version control records changes to project files and helps teams review or restore previous versions. Modern hosting services can deploy a website when changes are merged into a designated repository branch.

Practical Application

An automated workflow may build the site, run tests, and publish only after checks succeed. The principle is the same as manual deployment: release a verified version.

6.4 Deployment Verification and Rollback

Detailed lesson: Smoke tests are quick checks of critical features immediately after deployment. Verify the homepage, navigation, key forms, and downloads. If a critical function fails, use the rollback plan and investigate.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Practical Application

Verify HTTPS, the homepage, important links, form submissions, mobile layout, and error reporting. Keep rollback steps documented before release.

Chapter 7: WEBSITE MAINTENANCE

Chapter 7: WEBSITE MAINTENANCE

This chapter covers understanding website maintenance, maintenance teams and publishing, feedback and content updates, website performance monitoring, and infrastructure monitoring. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

7.1 Understanding Website Maintenance

Detailed lesson: Maintenance includes fixing defects, updating content, checking performance, renewing services, and improving security. It should be planned regularly rather than performed only when a user reports a problem.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Website maintenance includes the activities needed to preserve a site’s operational integrity. The supplied maintenance handbook groups them into publishing, quality assurance, feedback monitoring, performance monitoring, infrastructure monitoring, and change control.

Practical Application

A maintained website has current information, working features, reliable hosting, and a process for identifying and correcting problems.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

7.2 Maintenance Teams and Publishing

Detailed lesson: A publishing workflow should define who may edit content, who reviews changes, and who releases updates. Separating review from publication reduces accidental errors.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Maintenance work may involve an editor, content contributors, developers, designers, quality reviewers, feedback staff, and infrastructure support. Small websites may combine several roles without removing their responsibilities.

Practical Application

Chapter 7: WEBSITE MAINTENANCE · Continued

7.3 Feedback and Content Updates

Detailed lesson: User feedback reveals broken links, unclear instructions, and outdated material. Track requests, confirm their impact, and update the website without changing unrelated content.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

Visitor feedback can reveal broken pages, confusing instructions, missing information, and service problems. A controlled process collects, acknowledges, investigates, responds to, and archives feedback.

Practical Application

The source includes historical examples of a contact form, live chat, and satisfaction rating. These illustrate channels for collecting comments; modern interfaces may look different.

Key Considerations

7.4 Website Performance Monitoring

Detailed lesson: Monitoring tracks page speed, availability, errors, and resource usage. Compare results over time and investigate changes after releases. A single fast test does not guarantee consistently good performance.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Performance monitoring evaluates whether the website is meeting its goals. Measures may include visits, engagement, task completion, errors, loading time, and user satisfaction.

Practical Application

Use metrics that match the website’s purpose. For an educational site, successful access to lessons and downloads may matter more than raw page views.

Key Considerations

7.5 Infrastructure Monitoring

Infrastructure monitoring observes hosting availability, resource usage, server errors, certificate status, storage, and other technical conditions. Alerts can help maintainers respond before users are widely affected.

Practical Application

Monitor uptime and recurring error patterns. Review hosting logs carefully and avoid exposing private user information in reports.

Chapter 8: CHANGE CONTROL AND LONG-TERM OPERATIONS

Chapter 8: CHANGE CONTROL AND LONG-TERM OPERATIONS

This chapter covers website change control, backups and recovery, security and updates, and troubleshooting and continuous improvement. It connects the underlying concepts to practical website work and to the source examples where relevant.

8.1 Website Change Control

Detailed lesson: Change control records what will change, why it is needed, who approved it, and how it was tested. For significant changes, record a rollback procedure and communicate possible downtime.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Change control coordinates technical and content changes so that updates are reviewed, tested, approved, and recorded. It reduces the risk of unexpected damage to a live website.

Practical Application

For every important change, record its purpose, affected pages, approval, testing results, publication time, and rollback method.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

A change-control record should make it possible to understand who requested a change, why it was necessary, who approved it, what was tested, and when it became available to visitors.

8.2 Backups and Recovery

Detailed lesson: Backups should be stored independently and tested through restoration. For a static website, source files and deployment configuration may be enough to rebuild the site; dynamic websites also need data backups.

Practical perspective: For a team project, assign one member to make the change and another to review it. Record what changed and verify the live site before considering the task complete.

A backup is a recoverable copy of website files, databases, or configuration. A useful backup plan defines frequency, storage location, retention, access controls, and restoration testing.

Practical Application

Chapter 8: CHANGE CONTROL AND LONG-TERM OPERATIONS · Continued

Keep copies outside the production server when possible. A backup that has never been tested may fail when it is most needed.

Key Considerations

The correct procedure depends on the website’s size, users, technical platform, and institutional requirements. Keep records of decisions, test changes in an appropriate environment, and verify results from the visitor’s point of view. When using historical screenshots from the supplied material, focus on the underlying workflow rather than assuming that today’s interfaces are identical.

8.3 Security and Updates

Detailed lesson: Keep software, libraries, and account access up to date. Remove unused credentials, review permissions, and monitor security notices from providers. Updates should be tested before publication.

Practical perspective: For an ITVerse-style e-library, check that each book cover opens the correct reader, chapter navigation follows the intended order, and media loads correctly after deployment.

Maintenance includes updating software, reviewing access permissions, renewing certificates, protecting credentials, and monitoring suspicious activity. Security work should be continuous rather than a one-time setup.

Practical Application

Remove unused accounts, use strong authentication, apply supported patches, and review third-party dependencies before installing updates.

Key Considerations

8.4 Troubleshooting and Continuous Improvement

Detailed lesson: Troubleshoot by identifying the symptom, reproducing it, checking recent changes, and testing one likely cause at a time. Record the resolution so future maintenance becomes faster.

Practical perspective: For a school website project, keep a record of the expected result, the actual result, and the steps used to verify each change. This creates evidence that the website works beyond the developer’s computer.

Chapter 8: CHANGE CONTROL AND LONG-TERM OPERATIONS · Continued

Troubleshooting begins with observing symptoms and collecting evidence. Changes should be made carefully, tested, and documented. Lessons from incidents should improve future procedures.

Practical Application

If images disappear after deployment, inspect file paths, capitalization, server responses, and permissions. Fix the cause, retest, and add the failure to the release checklist.
